analysis.one_liner: Directs federal safety regulators to require cigarettes that extinguish themselves instead of starting fires.
analysis.headline: The bill — named for Representative Joe Moakley, who had championed the issue — was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2002 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Cigarettes are the top cause of deadly house fires in the United States — in 1998 alone, cigarette fires killed 903 people, injured about 2,450, and caused over $411 million in property damage, including nearly 100 children killed each year. This bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a national fire-safety standard requiring cigarettes to be designed to go out on their own if left unattended, using a test method already developed by federal scientists, and to block manufacturers from stockpiling old-style cigarettes before the rule took effect. It would have left tougher state laws and fire victims' lawsuits untouched, but it also specifically denied the Commission any broader authority over tobacco products. The bill never got past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the people most likely to die in cigarette-ignited fires: smokers who fall asleep, the children and other household members who live with them, renters and neighbors, and firefighters. The bill's own findings put the annual cost of doing nothing at $4.6 billion in lost lives and property, and cite prior federal studies showing the technical work for a standard was already complete. Property and casualty insurers would also gain through fewer fire claims, and states would keep the right to impose tougher rules of their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smokers' families, children, renters, and firefighters

how_it_helps.text: Cigarette-ignited fires are the leading cause of fire deaths in the United States; the bill's findings cite 903 deaths, 2,453 civilian injuries, and $411.7 million in property damage in 1998 alone, including nearly 100 children killed each year.

The bill requires every cigarette sold or imported to pass a self-extinguishing test — no more than 25 percent of test cigarettes may burn their full length without going out — using the testing method developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in earlier cigarette-safety studies.
It includes an anti-stockpiling provision barring manufacturers and importers from ramping up production of old-format cigarettes between the standard's issuance and its effective date.

The bill expressly does not preempt tougher state fire-safety laws and preserves private lawsuits under the Consumer Product Safety Act, so states and fire victims could go further than the federal standard.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen mainly on cigarette manufacturers, who would have had to redesign their products and cigarette paper so unattended cigarettes self-extinguish, verify each product through a standardized 40-replicate test, and comply with an anti-stockpiling rule that prevents flooding the market with old-format cigarettes before the deadline. Consumers would likely have shared some of that cost in prices. The bill authorized $2 million for the Commission to administer it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cigarette manufacturers, likely some pass-through to smokers

drawbacks.text: The bill is deliberately narrow: Section 5 says the Consumer Product Safety Commission 'shall have no jurisdiction over tobacco or tobacco products' beyond this fire-safety standard, so it does nothing to address the health harms of smoking itself — it makes cigarettes harder to start fires, not safer to smoke.

The mandate carries real compliance costs: manufacturers would have to redesign cigarettes and cigarette paper to pass the self-extinguishing test, verify each product in 40-replicate trials, and comply with the anti-stockpiling rule, and those costs are typically reflected in prices.

The 18-month deadline was aggressive for a rule covering every cigarette sold in the country, and the bill allows the agency to modify the standard only after the rule has been in effect three years, which limits early course-correction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side was modest and mostly fell on manufacturers: the bill's core burden was redesigning cigarettes with slower-burning paper and running the required tests, plus an anti-stockpiling rule to prevent a rush of old-format cigarettes before the deadline [S3]. The benefit side, per the bill's own findings, was large: cigarette fires killed over 900 people and injured about 2,450 in a single year, nearly 100 of them children, and the CPSC put the annual cost of having no standard at $4.6 billion [S3]. On paper this is a clear trade. The bill's honest limits are that it is narrow — it touches ignition only and specifically denies the regulator any general authority over tobacco [S3] — and, since it never became law, its benefits were never delivered at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2002 and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The complete action history shows only three steps: introduction on April 25, 2002, introductory remarks, and a second reading with referral to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — nothing after that.

The bill had built-in support for quick action: it cited completed technical work from the Cigarette Safety Act of 1984 and the Fire Safe Cigarette Act of 1990, meaning the testing method and acceptance criteria were already developed and waiting for a standard to be written.
The bill died with no roll-call vote ever taken in either chamber, so the public never got a record of who supported or opposed it on the merits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cigarette manufacturers came out ahead: no federal redesign mandate, testing requirement, or anti-stockpiling rule took effect, and no comparable federal standard was enacted during that Congress. The 900-plus people a year who die in cigarette-ignited fires gained nothing from this bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cigarette makers who avoided a redesign mandate

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat from Illinois joined by two Massachusetts Democrats and a Kansas Republican, with 5 of 49 Senate Democrats and 3 of 49 Senate Republicans signing on as cosponsors [S4] — but since no vote ever occurred, the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would force cigarette makers to redesign their products with self-extinguishing paper and pass a government ignition test, and would bar them from stockpiling old-format cigarettes before the deadline. The industry's interest was in avoiding that mandate, which runs against the public's interest in fewer fire deaths; the bill also locks in a narrow regulatory role, denying the CPSC any broader authority over tobacco.

Cigarette fires caused $411.7 million in property damage in 1998 by the bill's findings; a standard that reduces ignitions would cut fire losses insurers pay out. Their interest runs alongside the public's.
